subject: Civics
text: Explain any two Fundamental Rights guaranteed to the people of India in Part III of the Indian Constitution.
modelAnswer: Part III of the Constitution guarantees six Fundamental Rights. For example: (1) Right to Equality (Articles 14-18) - guarantees equality before law, prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, and abolishes untouchability and titles. (2) Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22) - guarantees six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession), along with protection against arbitrary arrest and punishment. Other rights include the Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and the Right to Constitutional Remedies.
keyPoints: Right to Equality: equality before law, no discrimination, abolition of untouchability
Right to Freedom: six freedoms including speech, assembly and movement
Other Fundamental Rights: against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural/Educational Rights, Constitutional Remedies

subject: Civics
text: State the main provisions of the Fundamental Right that guarantees religious freedom to the citizens of India.
modelAnswer: The Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28) guarantees that: (1) every citizen is free to profess, practise and propagate any religion of their choice, subject to public order, morality and health; (2) the State shall not discriminate on grounds of religion and may regulate secular activities associated with religious practice; (3) every religious denomination has the right to manage its own religious affairs and institutions; (4) no person can be compelled to pay any tax for the promotion of a particular religion; and (5) no religious instruction can be imparted in wholly State-funded educational institutions.
keyPoints: Freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion
No discrimination on grounds of religion; religious denominations manage their own affairs
No person compelled to pay tax for a particular religion; no religious instruction in wholly State-funded institutions

subject: Civics
text: Fundamental Duties are a set of moral and ethical obligations that citizens are expected to follow. State any three of them.
modelAnswer: Three of the Fundamental Duties listed under Article 51-A are: (1) to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem; (2) to cherish and follow the noble ideals that inspired the national struggle for freedom; (3) to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India. Other duties include protecting the natural environment, developing scientific temper, safeguarding public property, and striving towards excellence in all fields of activity.
keyPoints: Respect the Constitution, National Flag and National Anthem
Cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle
Uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; also protect environment and public property

subject: Civics
text: 'Indian Constitution makes Equality the bedrock of Indian polity.' Mention the constitutional provisions to ensure the same.
modelAnswer: The Right to Equality (Articles 14-18) ensures the following provisions: (1) Article 14 - equality before the law and equal protection of laws for all persons. (2) Article 15 - prohibition of discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. (3) Article 16 - equality of opportunity in matters of public employment. (4) Article 17 - abolition of untouchability in any form. (5) Article 18 - abolition of titles (except military and academic distinctions), preventing artificial social hierarchies.
keyPoints: Article 14: equality before law and equal protection of laws
Article 15 & 16: no discrimination; equal opportunity in public employment
Article 17 & 18: abolition of untouchability and of titles

subject: Civics
text: What does 'begar' mean, and name the Fundamental Right that prohibits begar or forced labour. Throw light on the other two provisions stated under this Fundamental Right.
modelAnswer: 'Begar' means forced labour extracted from a person without payment. It is prohibited under the Right against Exploitation (Articles 23 and 24). Besides prohibiting begar and traffic in human beings (Article 23), this Right also: (1) prohibits employment of children below 14 years of age in factories, mines or other hazardous occupations (Article 24); and (2) prohibits forced labour in any other form, protecting vulnerable and economically weaker sections from being exploited.
keyPoints: Begar = forced labour without payment
Prohibited under the Right against Exploitation (Articles 23 & 24)
Also prohibits traffic in human beings and employment of children below 14 in hazardous work

subject: Civics
text: What is the composition of the Election Commission of India? Give any two points explaining the significance of elections in a democracy like India.
modelAnswer: The Election Commission of India is a permanent constitutional body consisting of a Chief Election Commissioner and such number of other Election Commissioners as the President may fix from time to time, all appointed by the President of India. Significance of elections: (1) Elections allow citizens to choose their representatives and participate in the government of the country, making democracy a reality. (2) Elections hold the government accountable, since representatives who fail to perform can be voted out at the next election, ensuring responsible and responsive governance.
keyPoints: Composition: Chief Election Commissioner + other Election Commissioners, appointed by the President
Significance: lets citizens choose their representatives, giving effect to democracy
Significance: makes government accountable, since poor performance can be punished at the next election

subject: Civics
text: State the composition of the body responsible for conducting elections and the appointment of its members. Mention two ways in which the independence of the working of this body is ensured.
modelAnswer: The Election Commission of India consists of the Chief Election Commissioner and other Election Commissioners, all appointed by the President of India. Its independence is ensured by: (1) security of tenure - the Chief Election Commissioner can be removed only through an impeachment process similar to that of a Supreme Court judge, protecting him/her from arbitrary dismissal; and (2) fixed service conditions - his/her salary and conditions of service cannot be varied to his/her disadvantage after appointment, insulating the office from political pressure.
keyPoints: Composition: CEC and other Election Commissioners, appointed by the President
Independence: security of tenure - removal only by impeachment, as for a Supreme Court judge
Independence: service conditions/salary cannot be altered to disadvantage after appointment

subject: Civics
text: Define indirect election. Name the legislative posts filled by direct election and by indirect election respectively.
modelAnswer: Indirect election is a method in which voters do not directly elect their representatives; instead, they elect an intermediate body of representatives who in turn elect the officeholder. Posts filled by Direct Election: members of the Lok Sabha and members of the State Legislative Assemblies (Vidhan Sabha). Posts filled by Indirect Election: members of the Rajya Sabha (elected by State Legislative Assemblies), members of State Legislative Councils (Vidhan Parishad), and the President and Vice-President of India (elected by an Electoral College of legislators).
keyPoints: Indirect election: voters elect representatives who then elect the officeholder
Direct election: Lok Sabha and Vidhan Sabha members
Indirect election: Rajya Sabha, Vidhan Parishad members, President and Vice-President

subject: Civics
text: How are elections of the President and Vice-President of India held?
modelAnswer: The President of India is elected indirectly through an Electoral College consisting of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the Legislative Assemblies of the States and Union Territories with legislatures, using the system of proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote, through a secret ballot. The Vice-President is also elected indirectly, but by a smaller Electoral College consisting only of the members (elected and nominated) of both Houses of Parliament, following the same system of proportional representation and secret ballot; State legislators do not take part in this election.
keyPoints: President: elected by Electoral College of MPs + elected MLAs of States/UTs, by proportional representation/secret ballot
Vice-President: elected only by members of both Houses of Parliament
Both use the system of a single transferable vote by secret ballot

subject: Civics
text: 'Indian Elections are truly democratic in nature whether conducted directly or indirectly.' Mention the key differences between the two forms of elections.
modelAnswer: In Direct Election, voters themselves cast their votes to choose their representatives, as is done for the Lok Sabha and the State Vidhan Sabhas. In Indirect Election, voters first elect a body of representatives, who then go on to elect the officeholder on the voters' behalf; this method is used for the Rajya Sabha, the Vidhan Parishads, and the offices of the President and Vice-President. Though the process differs, both forms are considered democratic because ultimately all representatives involved can be traced back to the choice of the people.
keyPoints: Direct election: voters themselves choose their representatives (e.g. Lok Sabha, Vidhan Sabha)
Indirect election: voters elect representatives who then elect the officeholder (e.g. President, Rajya Sabha)
Both remain democratic since all electors trace back to the people's choice

subject: Civics
text: List any three ways that are followed to ensure free and fair elections in India.
modelAnswer: Free and fair elections in India are ensured through: (1) an independent Election Commission that is insulated from political pressure by security of tenure for the Chief Election Commissioner; (2) the use of secret ballot, so that voters can vote without fear or influence; (3) a Model Code of Conduct that regulates the campaigning, spending and conduct of political parties and candidates during elections, along with the use of EVMs and strict monitoring to prevent malpractice such as booth capturing or bribery.
keyPoints: Independent, insulated Election Commission
Secret ballot system
Model Code of Conduct and strict monitoring to prevent electoral malpractice

subject: Civics
text: With regard to the Panchayat Samiti, explain what is meant by the Panchayat Samiti and what different names are given to it in different states, and discuss its supervisory, civic and developmental functions.
modelAnswer: The Panchayat Samiti is the intermediate (block-level) tier of the three-tier Panchayati Raj system, linking the village-level Gram Panchayats to the district-level Zila Parishad. It is known by different names in different states, such as Block Samiti, Taluka Panchayat or Mandal Panchayat. Its supervisory functions include overseeing and coordinating the work of the Gram Panchayats within the block and reviewing their budgets and development plans. Its civic and developmental functions include setting up Anganwadis for child welfare, maintaining rural roads and water supply, implementing rural employment schemes like MGNREGA, and promoting agriculture, education and health programmes at the block level.
keyPoints: Panchayat Samiti: block-level (intermediate) tier of Panchayati Raj; also called Block/Taluka/Mandal Panchayat
Supervisory function: oversees and coordinates Gram Panchayats within the block
Civic/developmental functions: Anganwadis, roads, water supply, employment schemes like MGNREGA

subject: Civics
text: What is a Nyaya Panchayat? How does it ensure inexpensive justice to people, and what is its jurisdiction?
modelAnswer: A Nyaya Panchayat is the judicial wing of village-level local self-government, set up to settle minor civil and criminal disputes at the village level without the delay and expense of formal courts. It ensures inexpensive justice because lawyers are not allowed to represent either party, no court fees are charged, and cases are settled quickly by panch members who are familiar with the local people and customs. Its jurisdiction is limited to petty disputes - for example, small civil claims and minor criminal offences - and it can impose only small fines; it has no power to award imprisonment.
keyPoints: Nyaya Panchayat: judicial wing at village level, settles minor civil/criminal disputes
Ensures inexpensive justice: no lawyers allowed, no court fees, quick disposal
Jurisdiction limited to petty cases; can impose only small fines, not imprisonment

subject: Civics
text: Explain the three-tier structure of the Panchayati Raj Institutions.
modelAnswer: The Panchayati Raj system, recommended by the Balwant Rai Mehta Committee and given constitutional status by the 73rd Amendment Act, 1992, operates at three levels: (1) Gram Panchayat - the village-level body, elected by the Gram Sabha, that functions as the executive wing of the village. (2) Panchayat Samiti - the intermediate, block-level body that coordinates the work of several Gram Panchayats in the block. (3) Zila Parishad - the top, district-level body that coordinates and supervises the work of the Panchayat Samitis within the district, acting as a link between the state government and rural local bodies.
keyPoints: Gram Panchayat: village-level executive body
Panchayat Samiti: intermediate, block-level coordinating body
Zila Parishad: district-level body supervising Panchayat Samitis, links state government to rural bodies

subject: Civics
text: Discuss the civic facilities and welfare functions of the Zila Parishad.
modelAnswer: As the apex rural local body at the district level, the Zila Parishad performs civic and welfare functions such as: coordinating and supervising the development plans and budgets of all Panchayat Samitis in the district; managing and allocating government and state funds for rural development projects; overseeing the implementation of welfare schemes relating to education, health, and sanitation across the district; and advising the state government on matters of rural development and the needs of the district's villages.
keyPoints: Coordinates and supervises Panchayat Samitis' plans and budgets across the district
Manages and allocates funds for rural development projects
Oversees welfare schemes in education, health and sanitation; advises the state government

subject: Civics
text: What is a Gram Sabha? Who is the head of the Gram Panchayat, and how can the head be removed from office before completion of the term?
modelAnswer: A Gram Sabha is a general meeting of all the adult members (registered voters) of a village, which elects the Gram Panchayat and reviews its work. The head of the Gram Panchayat is usually called the Sarpanch (or Gram Pradhan). The Sarpanch can be removed from office before the completion of the term through a no-confidence motion passed by the required majority of elected Panchayat members, or by order of the state government if found guilty of misconduct, corruption, or misuse of office.
keyPoints: Gram Sabha: assembly of all adult voters of the village
Head of Gram Panchayat: the Sarpanch/Gram Pradhan
Removal: no-confidence motion by required majority, or state government order for misconduct

subject: Civics
text: State any four obligatory functions of the Municipal Corporations.
modelAnswer: Obligatory functions of Municipal Corporations include: (1) supplying safe drinking water to the city; (2) building and maintaining roads, drains and sewerage systems; (3) providing street lighting and maintaining public sanitation and cleanliness, including garbage collection; and (4) registering births and deaths, and maintaining public health through vaccination drives and hospitals/dispensaries. These are compulsory functions that a Corporation must perform for the basic welfare of its citizens.
keyPoints: Water supply and drainage/sewerage systems
Construction and maintenance of roads; street lighting and sanitation
Registration of births/deaths and public health services

subject: Civics
text: Describe any three discretionary functions of a Municipal Corporation.
modelAnswer: Discretionary functions are those a Municipal Corporation may choose to perform for the comfort, convenience and cultural life of citizens, rather than being compulsory. Examples include: (1) setting up and maintaining public libraries and museums; (2) developing parks, gardens and recreational facilities; (3) providing public transport facilities and constructing community halls or shopping centres for public use.
keyPoints: Discretionary functions are optional, unlike obligatory functions
Examples: public libraries and museums
Examples: parks/gardens, public transport, community halls

subject: History
text: What evidence shows that the Harappans participated in a vast maritime trade?
modelAnswer: Several pieces of evidence point to extensive Harappan maritime trade: (1) a well-built brick dockyard has been excavated at Lothal, which could accommodate ships and handle loading and unloading of goods; (2) Harappan seals, used to mark and identify traded goods, have been discovered at sites in distant Mesopotamia, showing trade links with that region; (3) depictions of boats and ships appear on some Harappan seals and artefacts; and (4) items like beads, pottery and finished goods found far from their place of origin suggest organised long-distance exchange, both within the subcontinent and overseas.
keyPoints: Dockyard excavated at Lothal for handling ships
Harappan seals discovered at distant Mesopotamian sites
Depictions of boats/ships on Harappan seals and artefacts; goods found far from their origin

subject: History
text: The seals are considered the most valuable historical finds of the Harappan Civilisation. Justify the statement.
modelAnswer: Harappan seals, usually made of steatite, are extremely valuable historical sources because: (1) they bear a pictographic script which, although still undeciphered, provides evidence that the Harappans were literate; (2) they are carved with animal motifs (such as the unicorn bull and bison), giving clues to the religious beliefs, flora and fauna of the time; (3) they were used to stamp and identify traded goods, proving the existence of an organised trade and commerce system; and (4) similar seals found in Mesopotamia establish that the Harappans had overseas trade links with that civilisation.
keyPoints: Bear pictographic (undeciphered) script, showing literacy
Animal motifs reveal religious beliefs and the environment of the time
Used in trade; discovery of similar seals in Mesopotamia proves overseas trade links

subject: History
text: State the differences in the position of women between the Early Vedic and Later Vedic Age.
modelAnswer: In the Early Vedic Age, women enjoyed a relatively higher status: they could attend tribal assemblies, receive education, perform religious sacrifices alongside men, and even compose Vedic hymns. In the Later Vedic Age, however, the position of women declined considerably: child marriage became more common, their access to education and participation in public assemblies was curtailed, polygamy increased among the wealthy, and they came to be regarded as subordinate to men in matters of property and religious ritual.
keyPoints: Early Vedic Age: women attended assemblies, received education, some composed hymns
Later Vedic Age: declining status - increased child marriage, restricted education and public role
Later Vedic Age: rise of polygamy and growing subordination of women in property/ritual matters

subject: History
text: Describe the Ashrama System of the Later Vedic Period.
modelAnswer: The Ashrama System divided a man's life into four stages. (1) Brahmacharya - the student stage, spent studying under a guru in a Gurukul, practising celibacy and discipline. (2) Grihastha - the householder stage, in which a man married, raised a family, and performed social and economic duties. (3) Vanaprastha - a stage of partial retirement, where he withdrew gradually from worldly life, often to the forest, while still guiding his family. (4) Sanyasa - the final stage, in which a man renounced all worldly ties to focus wholly on spiritual pursuits.
keyPoints: Brahmacharya: student life, education under a guru
Grihastha: householder life, family and social duties
Vanaprastha and Sanyasa: partial and then complete renunciation of worldly life

subject: History
text: Imagine you were born after 1000 BC to 500 BC, and explain what changes you would have noticed in the Varna system that was prevalent during that time.
modelAnswer: By 1000-500 BC (the Later Vedic period), the Varna system, which had originally been a flexible division of society based on occupation, became far more rigid. Membership of a Varna - Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya or Shudra - was now decided by birth rather than by occupation or personal merit, so a person's social position and rights became fixed from birth. The Brahmins and Kshatriyas gained increasing dominance and privilege, while the Shudras, who performed manual and menial work, were pushed to the lowest rung and faced growing restrictions, including on movement, intermarriage and access to religious rituals - the beginnings of untouchability.
keyPoints: Varna became based on birth rather than occupation or merit, unlike earlier flexibility
Brahmins and Kshatriyas gained greater dominance and privilege
Shudras faced growing restrictions, laying the foundation for untouchability

subject: History
text: Explain three causes which contributed to the growth of discontent against the Vedic religion in the 6th century BC.
modelAnswer: Discontent against the Vedic religion grew due to several factors: (1) the domineering attitude of the Brahmins, who claimed sole authority over religious rituals and demanded elaborate, costly sacrifices, alienating ordinary people; (2) the increasing rigidity of the caste system and the growth of untouchability, which denied the lower castes any religious or social dignity; and (3) the indiscriminate killing of cattle in large-scale Vedic sacrifices, which harmed the new agricultural economy that depended on cattle for ploughing, causing resentment among the farming communities. These factors together created fertile ground for new, simpler religious movements like Jainism and Buddhism.
keyPoints: Domineering attitude of Brahmins and costly, elaborate rituals
Rigid caste system and rise of untouchability
Cattle sacrifices harming the agricultural economy, causing resentment

subject: History
text: Who were the founders of the two religious reform movements of 6th century BC India? What were the similarities between their teachings?
modelAnswer: The two major religious reform movements of 6th century BC India were Jainism, founded by Vardhamana Mahavira, and Buddhism, founded by Gautama Buddha. Similarities between their teachings: (1) both rejected the authority of the Vedas and the dominance of Brahmin priests in religious matters; (2) both opposed the rigid caste system and emphasised that spiritual liberation was open to people of all social classes, through personal conduct rather than birth; (3) both preached non-violence (Ahimsa) and compassion towards all living beings, and condemned animal sacrifice; and (4) both encouraged the use of common (Prakrit/Pali) languages, rather than Sanskrit, to spread their teachings to ordinary people.
keyPoints: Jainism founded by Mahavira; Buddhism founded by Gautama Buddha
Both rejected Vedic ritualism and Brahmin dominance, opposed rigid caste system
Both preached non-violence and used common languages (Prakrit/Pali) to reach the masses

subject: History
text: Examine the Tripitakas as a source for reconstructing the religious reform movement of Buddhism.
modelAnswer: The Tripitakas ('Three Baskets'), written in Pali, are the chief canonical texts of Buddhism and a key source for reconstructing its history. They consist of: (1) the Vinaya Pitaka, which lays down the rules and code of conduct for monks and nuns of the Buddhist Sangha; (2) the Sutta Pitaka, which records the Buddha's sermons, sayings, and teachings on subjects like karma and rebirth; and (3) the Abhidhamma Pitaka, which contains philosophical analysis and interpretation of Buddhist doctrine. Together, these texts provide detailed insight into the Buddha's teachings, the organisation of the Sangha, and the early practice of Buddhism.
keyPoints: Tripitakas: 'Three Baskets' of Buddhist canonical texts, written in Pali
Vinaya Pitaka: monastic rules; Sutta Pitaka: Buddha's sermons and teachings
Abhidhamma Pitaka: philosophical doctrine; together they reveal teachings and organisation of the Sangha

subject: History
text: With reference to King Ashoka of the Mauryan Empire, explain the Kalinga War, the inscriptions on his pillars, and the fundamental principles of his Dhamma.
modelAnswer: The Kalinga War (261 BC) was Ashoka's bloody conquest of the kingdom of Kalinga; the enormous suffering and loss of life he witnessed deeply moved him and became the turning point of his reign, after which he embraced Buddhism and renounced warfare. Ashoka inscribed his edicts on pillars erected across his empire, often topped with animal capitals (like the famous lion capital at Sarnath); these pillar edicts spread his message of Dhamma to his subjects. The fundamental principles of his Dhamma included non-violence (Ahimsa), tolerance of all religions, truthfulness, respect for elders, ascetics and animals, and the welfare of all living beings - a code of ethical conduct rather than a new religion.
keyPoints: Kalinga War (261 BC): bloodshed that turned Ashoka towards Buddhism and non-violence
Pillar inscriptions: edicts spreading Dhamma, carrying animal capitals like the Sarnath lion capital
Dhamma principles: non-violence, tolerance, truthfulness, respect for elders and welfare of all beings

subject: History
text: Give evidence to suggest the excellent administration of the city of Patliputra, as described in Megasthenes's 'Indica'.
modelAnswer: Megasthenes, in his account 'Indica', described Patliputra, the Mauryan capital, as a well-fortified and well-administered city. He noted that the city's municipal administration was run by six committees (boards), each responsible for a different civic function such as sanitation, trade and commerce, care of foreigners, registration of births and deaths, and maintenance of public buildings. He also described wide, well-planned streets, strong wooden fortifications with watchtowers, and an efficient espionage and policing system that maintained law and order in the city.
keyPoints: Megasthenes's 'Indica' describes Patliputra as well-fortified and well-administered
Six municipal committees managed functions like sanitation, trade, and care of foreigners
Well-planned streets, strong fortifications, and efficient policing/espionage system

subject: History
text: Provide a detailed account of the Gupta administration with regard to Provincial Administration and the Administration of Law and Justice.
modelAnswer: Note: this combines Gupta provincial and judicial administration. Provincial Administration - the Gupta Empire was divided into provinces called 'Bhuktis', each headed by an 'Uparika', usually a prince or trusted official appointed by the king. Bhuktis were further divided into districts ('Vishayas'), governed by a 'Vishyapati', and villages were administered by a headman called the 'Gramika'. Administration of Law and Justice - the king was the highest court of justice and the final authority on legal matters, assisted by judicial officers; however, much of the day-to-day justice at the local level was administered by village and town councils and guilds, based on customary law, and punishments, as noted by the Chinese traveller Fa-hien, were generally mild rather than harsh.
keyPoints: Provinces (Bhuktis) headed by Uparikas; districts (Vishayas) headed by Vishyapatis; villages by Gramikas
King was the highest judicial authority, assisted by officials
Local disputes often settled by village/town councils and guilds; punishments generally mild (per Fa-hien)

subject: History
text: 'Aryabhata, an ancient Indian mathematician and astronomer, made many contributions to the fields of mathematics and astronomy.' Justify the statement.
modelAnswer: Aryabhatta made remarkable contributions to science during the Gupta period: (1) in mathematics, he calculated the value of pi to a close approximation and made advances in algebra, trigonometry, and the place-value system; (2) in astronomy, he correctly explained that solar and lunar eclipses are caused by the shadows of the earth and moon, not by mythical demons as popularly believed; (3) he proposed that the earth is spherical and rotates on its own axis, which explains day and night; and (4) he wrote two major works, the 'Aryabhatiya' and the 'Surya Siddhanta', which remained influential in Indian astronomy for centuries.
keyPoints: Mathematics: close calculation of pi; advances in algebra and trigonometry
Astronomy: correct scientific explanation of solar and lunar eclipses
Proposed earth's rotation on its axis; wrote the Aryabhatiya and Surya Siddhanta

subject: History
text: 'Samudragupta is regarded as the Indian Napoleon.' Why?
modelAnswer: Samudragupta is called the 'Indian Napoleon' because, like the French general Napoleon Bonaparte, he was an unrivalled military conqueror who greatly expanded his empire through successful campaigns. He defeated numerous kings in Aryavarta (northern India) and the Dakshinapatha (southern India), bringing many rulers under his suzerainty, and is said to have never been defeated in battle throughout his long reign. The Allahabad Pillar Inscription, composed by his court poet Harisena, records his extensive military conquests in detail, justifying the comparison with Napoleon.
keyPoints: Like Napoleon, Samudragupta was an unrivalled, undefeated military conqueror
Defeated numerous kings in northern and southern India, expanding the Gupta empire greatly
His conquests are recorded in detail in the Allahabad Pillar Inscription by Harisena

subject: History
text: 'In the Sangam Age, Agriculture and Trade were in a flourishing stage.' Justify the statement.
modelAnswer: During the Sangam Age, agriculture flourished in the fertile river valleys of South India, especially along the Krishna and Tungabhadra, where rice was the staple crop, supported by developed irrigation using tanks and canals. Trade was equally prosperous: South Indian kingdoms exported pepper (called 'Yavanpriya' for its popularity with Roman traders), pearls, gems, textiles, and spices through flourishing port towns such as Puhar and Muziris, in exchange for Roman gold coins and wine. This vibrant maritime trade with Rome and South-East Asia brought great wealth to the Sangam kingdoms.
keyPoints: Agriculture: rice cultivation in fertile river valleys, supported by tank/canal irrigation
Trade: export of pepper, pearls, gems and textiles through ports like Puhar and Muziris
Flourishing maritime trade with Rome, exchanging goods for gold and wine, brought great wealth

subject: History
text: Describe the division of castes/social classes among the Tamil people in the Sangam Age.
modelAnswer: Sangam-age Tamil society was divided into social classes rather than the rigid Varna system of the north. The ruling class (chiefs and kings, called 'Vendar' or 'Arasar') stood at the top, followed by the 'Vellalar', a class of land-owning agriculturists who formed the backbone of the rural economy and enjoyed considerable social status. There were also traders and craftsmen who gained in importance due to flourishing overseas trade, and labouring and artisan classes who performed various essential occupations. Compared to the northern Varna system, Sangam society was somewhat more flexible, with social mobility linked to occupation and wealth.
keyPoints: Ruling class (Vendar/Arasar - chiefs and kings) at the top
Vellalar: land-owning agriculturist class, backbone of the rural economy
Traders, craftsmen and labouring classes; more flexible than the northern Varna system

subject: History
text: 'The Chola Period is remarkable for the efficiency of its village institutions.' Enumerate.
modelAnswer: Chola village administration was remarkably organised through local self-governing assemblies: the 'Ur' was the general assembly of all villagers; the 'Sabha' (or Mahasabha) was an assembly specific to Brahmin villages (Brahmadeya), with wider powers; and the 'Nagaram' was an assembly of merchants in trading towns. These assemblies managed local affairs through specialised sub-committees called 'Variyams', which handled specific duties such as irrigation and tank maintenance, justice, temple administration, and revenue collection, allowing considerable local autonomy and efficient grassroots governance - a system often cited as an early form of local self-government.
keyPoints: Ur: general village assembly; Sabha: Brahmin village assembly with wider powers
Nagaram: assembly of merchants in trading towns
Variyams (sub-committees) managed irrigation, justice, temple administration and revenue - giving local autonomy

subject: History
text: What were the military achievements of Rajendra I Chola?
modelAnswer: Rajendra I, son of Rajaraja I, was a great Chola military conqueror. His main achievements include: (1) a victorious northern expedition that reached the river Ganga, after which he adopted the title 'Gangaikonda' and founded a new capital, Gangaikondacholapuram, to commemorate the victory; (2) successful naval expeditions against the Srivijaya empire (covering parts of present-day Java, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula), establishing Chola naval supremacy over South-East Asian trade routes; and (3) military campaigns that brought Ceylon (Sri Lanka) and the Maldive Islands under Chola influence.
keyPoints: Northern expedition to the Ganga; adopted title 'Gangaikonda', founded Gangaikondacholapuram
Naval expedition against Srivijaya (Java, Sumatra, Malay Peninsula)
Brought Ceylon and the Maldives under Chola influence

subject: History
text: Muhammad bin Tughlaq is famous in history more because of his failures than his successes. In this context, explain his decision of introducing token currency, his decision on raising taxes in the Doab, and his decision on shifting the capital.
modelAnswer: Muhammad bin Tughlaq undertook three bold but disastrous experiments: (1) Token Currency - he introduced copper/brass coins to be valued at par with silver to deal with a shortage of precious metal, but since the coins were easily forged and lacked adequate safeguards, counterfeiters flooded the market, destroying public trust and forcing him to withdraw the scheme at heavy loss to the treasury. (2) Taxation in the Doab - he sharply raised land taxes in the fertile Doab region at a time when it was already suffering from famine; the harsh, insensitive enforcement caused widespread peasant distress and rebellion. (3) Transfer of Capital - he shifted the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad in the Deccan for strategic reasons, forcing the entire population to migrate over a long and difficult journey, only to move the capital back to Delhi a few years later, causing immense hardship and loss of life with no lasting benefit.
keyPoints: Token currency: easily-forged coins led to counterfeiting and collapse of the scheme
Doab taxation: harsh tax increase during famine caused peasant rebellion
Transfer of capital to Daulatabad: forced migration, hardship, later reversed - all with no lasting gain

subject: History
text: Explain the features of the Central Administration of the Sultanate Period.
modelAnswer: The Central Administration of the Delhi Sultanate was headed by the Sultan, who held supreme military, executive, and judicial authority, assisted by a council of ministers. Key ministers included the Wazir, who headed the finance department and managed revenue; the Ariz-i-Mumalik, who was in charge of the army and military affairs; the Sadr-us-Sadr, who looked after religious and charitable matters; and the Qazi-ul-Quzat, the chief justice, who headed the judicial department. This centralised structure allowed the Sultan to maintain control over a large empire through specialised departments.
keyPoints: Sultan: supreme head with military, executive and judicial authority
Wazir: finance minister; Ariz-i-Mumalik: in charge of the army
Sadr-us-Sadr: religious/charitable affairs; Qazi-ul-Quzat: chief justice

subject: History
text: Name the Sultan who was most successful in implementing market control policy, and explain his reforms initiated for market regulation.
modelAnswer: Alauddin Khalji was the Sultan who most successfully implemented market control reforms. His measures included: (1) fixing the prices of essential commodities such as grain, cloth, and horses, which were strictly enforced; (2) maintaining state granaries that stored grain to be released during times of scarcity, preventing hoarding and price rises; (3) appointing a market controller known as the 'Shahna-i-Mandi' to supervise the markets and ensure fair dealing; and (4) employing spies to secretly report on prices and the quality of goods sold, with severe punishment for those who violated the regulations. These reforms kept prices stable and were especially important for maintaining a large, affordable standing army.
keyPoints: Alauddin Khalji: most successful at market-control reforms
Fixed prices of essential goods; maintained state granaries against scarcity
Appointed Shahna-i-Mandi to supervise markets; used spies to monitor prices and quality

subject: History
text: Discuss the policies adopted by Akbar which acquired him the title of 'Akbar the Great'.
modelAnswer: Akbar earned the title 'Akbar the Great' through several far-sighted policies: (1) religious tolerance - he abolished the jizya tax on non-Muslims, ended forced conversions, and even founded a new faith, Din-i-Ilahi, that drew from several religions, winning the loyalty of his diverse subjects; (2) administrative reforms - he introduced the Mansabdari system, which organised nobles and officers into ranks tied to their military obligations, creating an efficient and disciplined administration; (3) matrimonial alliances - he formed marriage alliances with Rajput princesses, securing the loyalty of powerful Rajput clans; and (4) military conquests - he expanded the Mughal Empire significantly through successful campaigns, consolidating a vast and stable realm.
keyPoints: Religious tolerance: abolished jizya, ended forced conversions, founded Din-i-Ilahi
Mansabdari system: efficient, disciplined administration
Rajput matrimonial alliances; extensive and successful military conquests

subject: History
text: Enumerate any four architectural features of the Taj Mahal.
modelAnswer: The Taj Mahal at Agra, built by Shah Jahan, displays several notable architectural features: (1) it is built entirely of white marble, brought from Makrana in Rajasthan, which gives the monument its luminous appearance; (2) it stands on a raised platform within a symmetrical Charbagh (four-part) garden, reflecting Persian garden design; (3) it has a large central dome flanked by four slender minarets at its corners, creating perfect architectural symmetry; and (4) its surfaces are decorated with intricate 'Pietra Dura' (inlay work using precious and semi-precious stones) and elegant calligraphy of verses from the Quran.
keyPoints: Built entirely of white marble from Makrana, Rajasthan
Raised platform within a symmetrical Charbagh garden
Central dome with four minarets; Pietra Dura inlay work and Quranic calligraphy

subject: History
text: Explain the significance of the Bhakti Movement in bringing about harmony between Hindus and Muslims.
modelAnswer: The Bhakti Movement played a significant role in promoting Hindu-Muslim harmony. Saints such as Kabir and Guru Nanak taught that there was one formless God common to all religions, rejecting the rigid rituals and external distinctions of both Hinduism and Islam. They preached in the common people's languages rather than Sanskrit or Arabic/Persian, making their message accessible across communities. By emphasising devotion, love, equality, and the rejection of caste and religious bigotry, the movement created a shared spiritual culture that bridged the gap between Hindus and Muslims.
keyPoints: Saints like Kabir and Guru Nanak preached one formless God common to all
Teachings in common languages, accessible to people of all communities
Emphasis on devotion, equality and rejection of caste/religious bigotry fostered shared culture

subject: History
text: By whom is Christianity believed to have been introduced in India? State any three contributions of St. Francis Xavier in the advancement of Christianity in India.
modelAnswer: Christianity is traditionally believed to have been introduced in India by St. Thomas the Apostle, who is said to have arrived on the Malabar (Kerala) coast in the 1st century AD. St. Francis Xavier's contributions in later centuries include: (1) he worked extensively in Goa as a Jesuit missionary, converting many people to Christianity and establishing a strong Christian community there; (2) he set up schools and worked for the education and welfare of the local population, especially the poor; and (3) he is remembered for his missionary zeal and travels across South and Southeast Asia to spread Christianity, for which he was later canonised as a saint and became the patron saint of Goa.
keyPoints: Christianity believed introduced by St. Thomas the Apostle on the Malabar coast
St. Francis Xavier: extensive missionary work and conversions in Goa
Set up schools for education/welfare of the poor; canonised as a saint, patron saint of Goa

subject: History
text: Describe three causes of the Renaissance.
modelAnswer: The Renaissance in Europe was brought about by several factors: (1) the Crusades brought Europeans into contact with the advanced and sophisticated Arab and Byzantine civilisations, exposing them to classical Greek and Roman learning that had been preserved there; (2) the fall of Constantinople in 1453 forced many Greek scholars to flee to Italy, bringing with them classical manuscripts and reviving interest in Greek philosophy, art, and literature; and (3) the invention of the printing press by Gutenberg allowed ideas and classical texts to be reproduced and spread rapidly and cheaply across Europe, fuelling intellectual curiosity. The patronage of wealthy merchant families, such as the Medici of Florence, also supported artists and scholars during this period.
keyPoints: Crusades exposed Europeans to preserved classical Greek/Roman learning
Fall of Constantinople (1453): Greek scholars fled to Italy with classical manuscripts
Invention of the printing press spread ideas rapidly; patronage of wealthy families like the Medici

subject: History
text: The Renaissance in Europe ushered in a new era in literature. Illustrate the statement.
modelAnswer: The Renaissance brought about a new era in literature in several ways: writers began composing in vernacular (common) languages such as Italian and English, rather than only in Latin, making literature accessible to a wider audience. Humanist themes - celebrating human achievement, emotion, and individual experience rather than purely religious subjects - became central to literary works. This period produced great writers such as Dante (Divine Comedy), Petrarch (sonnets), and later William Shakespeare in England, whose plays like Hamlet, Macbeth and Romeo and Juliet explored deep human emotions and remain celebrated classics of world literature.
keyPoints: Shift to writing in vernacular languages rather than only Latin
Humanist themes celebrating individual human experience, not just religious subjects
Produced great writers: Dante, Petrarch, and Shakespeare (Hamlet, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet)

subject: History
text: Discuss any two effects that the invention of the printing press had on the lives of people during the Renaissance era.
modelAnswer: The printing press had far-reaching effects on Renaissance society: (1) it made books far cheaper and quicker to produce than hand-copied manuscripts, so that literacy and access to knowledge spread rapidly among the common people, not just the clergy and nobility; and (2) it allowed books to be printed in vernacular languages, which let ordinary people read the Bible and other texts for themselves rather than relying solely on priests, encouraging independent thought that later fuelled movements such as the Reformation.
keyPoints: Made books cheaper and faster to produce, spreading literacy widely
Enabled printing in vernacular languages, giving ordinary people direct access to texts
Encouraged independent thinking, later fuelling movements like the Reformation

subject: History
text: Identify and explain any four causes that led to the revolt against the Catholic Church.
modelAnswer: The revolt against the Catholic Church, which led to the Protestant Reformation, was caused by several factors: (1) the sale of indulgences - the Church sold pardons for sins to raise money, which many saw as corrupt and exploitative, exemplified by John Tetzel's campaign at Wittenberg; (2) the wealth and worldly lifestyle of the clergy and Popes, which contrasted sharply with the simple, humble life preached in the Gospels; (3) the political ambitions of the Popes, who behaved like secular rulers and interfered in the politics of European kingdoms, provoking resentment from kings and nobles; and (4) the invention of the printing press, which spread critical writings - such as those of Martin Luther and Erasmus - questioning Church practices to a much wider audience than before.
keyPoints: Sale of indulgences seen as corrupt (e.g. John Tetzel's campaign)
Worldly wealth and lifestyle of clergy and Popes contrasting with Gospel teachings
Political ambitions of Popes; printing press spreading critical writings widely

subject: History
text: What do you understand by the term 'Reformation'? Mention any two contributions of Martin Luther to the movement.
modelAnswer: The Reformation was a 16th-century religious movement aimed at reforming the practices and doctrines of the Catholic Church, which eventually led to a permanent split and the rise of Protestant churches in Europe. Martin Luther's contributions: (1) he wrote and nailed his Ninety-Five Theses to the church door at Wittenberg, listing his objections to Church practices, especially the sale of indulgences; and (2) he publicly burnt the Pope's Bull of Excommunication at Wittenberg in 1520, openly defying papal authority and encouraging others to break away from the Catholic Church, giving a major impetus to the Protestant movement.
keyPoints: Reformation: 16th-century movement to reform the Catholic Church, leading to Protestantism
Martin Luther: wrote and nailed the Ninety-Five Theses at Wittenberg
Martin Luther: publicly burnt the Papal Bull of Excommunication in 1520, defying the Pope

subject: History
text: Why did Martin Luther object to the power of the Pope? What measures were taken to introduce reforms in the Catholic Church?
modelAnswer: Martin Luther objected to the Pope's power because he believed the Church had strayed from the teachings of the Bible - particularly the sale of indulgences for forgiveness of sins, which he saw as a corrupt practice that had no basis in scripture, and the Pope's claim to absolute spiritual authority over all Christians. In response to the growing criticism, the Catholic Church undertook its own Counter-Reformation: it convened the Council of Trent to clarify and reaffirm Catholic doctrine and curb abuses such as the sale of indulgences; it approved the founding of new religious orders, notably the Jesuits (Society of Jesus) under Ignatius Loyola, to spread Catholic teaching and education; and it set up mechanisms like the Index of banned books to control the spread of ideas considered heretical.
keyPoints: Luther objected to sale of indulgences and the Pope's claim to absolute spiritual authority
Counter-Reformation: Council of Trent reaffirmed doctrine and curbed abuses
Founding of the Jesuit order; introduction of the Index of banned books

subject: History
text: Differentiate between Capitalism and Socialism with regard to Profit Maximisation versus Social Cohesion.
modelAnswer: Capitalism is an economic system in which private individuals and firms own the means of production and aim primarily at profit maximisation, with prices and production decided by market forces of demand and supply. Socialism, in contrast, emphasises social cohesion and the collective welfare of society over individual profit; production and distribution of resources are planned and often controlled by the state, with the goal of ensuring a more equitable sharing of wealth among all members of society rather than maximising profit for a few.
keyPoints: Capitalism: private ownership, profit maximisation, market-driven production
Socialism: emphasis on social cohesion and collective welfare over individual profit
Socialism: state-planned production/distribution aiming at equitable sharing of wealth

subject: History
text: Discuss the differences between Capitalism and Socialism with regard to Market Economy and Planned Economy.
modelAnswer: Under Capitalism, a Market Economy prevails, where prices, production and distribution of goods are determined mainly by the free interaction of demand and supply, with minimal government interference, allowing individuals and businesses to compete freely for profit. Under Socialism, a Planned Economy is followed, where the state plays a central role in deciding what is produced, how it is distributed, and at what price, with the explicit aim of meeting the needs of society and reducing economic inequality, rather than leaving these decisions purely to market forces.
keyPoints: Capitalism: Market Economy driven by demand and supply, minimal government role
Socialism: Planned Economy with the state deciding production and distribution
Socialism aims to meet societal needs and reduce inequality, unlike free-market competition

subject: Civics
text: Why is India considered a secular state?
modelAnswer: India is a secular state because the State has no official religion of its own and treats all religions equally. The Constitution guarantees every person the freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate any religion (Articles 25-28), and the State cannot discriminate against any citizen on grounds of religion. No religious instruction can be given in educational institutions wholly maintained by the State. The word "secular" was added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.
keyPoints: No official state religion; all religions treated equally
Freedom of religion guaranteed (Articles 25-28)
No discrimination on grounds of religion
Word "secular" added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976)

subject: Civics
text: Define Constitution. What does a Constitution determine?
modelAnswer: A Constitution is the fundamental law of a country: a set of basic rules and principles according to which the country is governed. It determines (1) the structure of the government and the powers and functions of its three organs, the legislature, the executive and the judiciary; (2) the relationship between these organs and between the Union and the States; and (3) the relationship between the government and the people, by laying down the rights and duties of citizens.
keyPoints: Constitution: the fundamental law / basic rules by which a country is governed
Determines the structure, powers and functions of the legislature, executive and judiciary
Defines relations between the organs and between the Union and the States
Lays down rights and duties of citizens

subject: Civics
text: State any three freedoms given under the Right to Freedom.
modelAnswer: Article 19 of the Constitution gives all citizens six freedoms: (1) freedom of speech and expression; (2) freedom to assemble peaceably and without arms; (3) freedom to form associations or unions; (4) freedom to move freely throughout the territory of India; (5) freedom to reside and settle in any part of India; and (6) freedom to practise any profession or to carry on any occupation, trade or business. These freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions in the interest of the security and public order of the country.
keyPoints: Freedom of speech and expression
Freedom to assemble peacefully without arms
Freedom to form associations or unions
Freedom to move, reside and settle anywhere in India
Freedom to practise any profession, trade or business

subject: Civics
text: Define a writ, mention any two types of writs, and state one situation in which a writ can be issued.
modelAnswer: A writ is a formal written order issued by the Supreme Court (under Article 32) or a High Court (under Article 226) commanding a person or authority to do, or not to do, something, in order to enforce the Fundamental Rights. Types of writs include Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari and Quo Warranto. For example, if a person is arrested and detained illegally, the court can issue a writ of Habeas Corpus ordering that the person be produced before it, and release the person if the detention is found unlawful.
keyPoints: Writ: written order of the Supreme Court or a High Court to enforce Fundamental Rights
Types: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, Quo Warranto
Example: Habeas Corpus in case of illegal detention

subject: Civics
text: Mention any two principles according to which elections are conducted in India.
modelAnswer: (1) Universal Adult Franchise: every citizen aged 18 years or above has the right to vote, regardless of caste, religion, sex, wealth or education. (2) Secret ballot: a voter casts the vote in secret so that no one knows whom he or she voted for, allowing voting without fear. (3) Single-member territorial constituencies, with seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes, and the candidate getting the most votes being declared elected.
keyPoints: Universal Adult Franchise (18 years and above)
Secret ballot
Single-member constituencies; reserved seats for SC/ST

subject: Civics
text: Explain any three functions of the Election Commission of India.
modelAnswer: The Election Commission (1) prepares and revises the electoral rolls (voters' lists) and issues voter identity cards; (2) prepares the schedule of elections, receives and scrutinises nomination papers and conducts the polls and counting of votes; (3) recognises political parties as national or state parties and allots election symbols to them; and (4) enforces the Model Code of Conduct and can order a re-poll or cancel an election in case of malpractice.
keyPoints: Prepares and revises electoral rolls; issues voter ID cards
Fixes election schedule, scrutinises nominations, conducts polling and counting
Recognises political parties and allots symbols
Enforces Model Code of Conduct; orders re-poll if needed

subject: Civics
text: State any two functions each of (i) the Gram Panchayat and (ii) the Panchayat Samiti.
modelAnswer: (i) Gram Panchayat: it provides civic amenities in the village such as clean drinking water, drainage and sanitation, street lighting and village roads; it maintains records of births and deaths; and it looks after primary health centres, primary schools and community centres. (ii) Panchayat Samiti: it coordinates and supervises the work of the Gram Panchayats in its block; and it implements development programmes in agriculture, irrigation, animal husbandry, cottage industries, primary health and education, and the welfare of Scheduled Castes and Tribes.
keyPoints: Gram Panchayat: drinking water, sanitation, street lights, village roads
Gram Panchayat: records of births/deaths, primary health and schools
Panchayat Samiti: coordinates and supervises Gram Panchayats
Panchayat Samiti: carries out block-level development schemes (agriculture, irrigation, cottage industries, welfare)

subject: Civics
text: Mention two key points of difference between the powers and functions of the upper house and the lower house of a State Legislature.
modelAnswer: (1) A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Legislative Assembly (lower house); the Legislative Council (upper house) cannot reject it and can delay it for only 14 days. (2) The Council of Ministers is responsible only to the Legislative Assembly, which can remove it by a vote of no-confidence; the Council has no such power. (3) In ordinary bills, the Assembly has the final say, as the Council can only delay a bill (up to three months the first time and one month the second time).
keyPoints: Money Bills only in the Assembly; Council can delay them only 14 days
Council of Ministers responsible only to the Assembly (no-confidence motion)
On ordinary bills the Council can only delay; the Assembly prevails

subject: Civics
text: Briefly explain any two limitations on the legislative powers of a State Legislature.
modelAnswer: (1) A State Legislature can make laws only on subjects in the State List and the Concurrent List; if a state law on a Concurrent subject conflicts with a law made by Parliament, the Union law prevails. (2) The Governor can reserve certain bills passed by the State Legislature for the consideration of the President, who may withhold assent. (3) During a National Emergency, or when the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution in the national interest, Parliament can make laws even on subjects in the State List.
keyPoints: Laws only on State and Concurrent List; Union law prevails in conflict
Governor may reserve bills for the President's assent
During Emergency or by Rajya Sabha resolution, Parliament can legislate on State List

subject: Civics
text: Explain the composition of the State Legislative Council and how its members are chosen.
modelAnswer: The members of the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad) are chosen as follows: (1) one-third are elected by the members of the Legislative Assembly from among persons who are not members of the Assembly; (2) one-third are elected by members of local bodies such as municipalities and panchayati raj institutions; (3) one-twelfth are elected by graduates of at least three years' standing residing in the state; (4) one-twelfth are elected by teachers of at least three years' standing in secondary schools and higher institutions; and (5) one-sixth are nominated by the Governor from persons with special knowledge of literature, science, art, the co-operative movement and social service. The strength of the Council cannot exceed one-third of the strength of the Assembly and cannot be less than 40.
keyPoints: 1/3 elected by MLAs from non-members
1/3 elected by members of local bodies
1/12 by graduates and 1/12 by teachers
1/6 nominated by the Governor
Strength: not more than 1/3 of Assembly, not less than 40

subject: Civics
text: What is a unicameral legislature and a bicameral legislature? Name one state with each.
modelAnswer: A unicameral legislature has only one House; in a state this is the Legislative Assembly (Vidhan Sabha), e.g. Tamil Nadu, Kerala or West Bengal. A bicameral legislature has two Houses; in a state these are the Legislative Assembly (lower house) and the Legislative Council (Vidhan Parishad, upper house), e.g. Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar or Karnataka.
keyPoints: Unicameral: one House (Legislative Assembly only)
Example of unicameral: Tamil Nadu / Kerala
Bicameral: two Houses (Assembly and Legislative Council)
Example of bicameral: Maharashtra / Uttar Pradesh

subject: Civics
text: Mention any two legislative powers of the State Legislature. What role does it play in the process of amending the Constitution?
modelAnswer: Legislative powers: (1) The State Legislature makes laws on all subjects in the State List, such as police, public health, agriculture and local government. (2) It can also make laws on subjects in the Concurrent List, such as education and forests, subject to Union laws. (3) It passes the state budget and Money Bills. Role in amendment: amendments that affect the federal structure, such as the election of the President, the distribution of legislative powers between the Union and the States, the representation of States in Parliament or the High Courts, must be passed by Parliament by a special majority and also be ratified by the legislatures of at least half of the States.
keyPoints: Makes laws on State List subjects
Makes laws on Concurrent List subjects (Union law prevails in conflict)
Passes the state budget/Money Bills
Ratification by at least half the State Legislatures needed for amendments affecting federal provisions

subject: History
text: State two pieces of evidence to prove that the Harappans paid great attention to health and sanitation.
modelAnswer: (1) The Harappan cities had an excellent drainage system: covered brick drains ran along the streets, with manholes for cleaning, and were connected to drains from every house. (2) Most houses had their own bathrooms and wells, and public bathing places such as the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro were built. (3) Rubbish was collected in bins or soak pits, keeping the streets clean.
keyPoints: Covered street drains with manholes, connected to house drains
Private bathrooms and wells; the Great Bath
Garbage bins and soak pits

subject: History
text: If you were a member of a lower caste in the 6th century BC, what aspects of Jainism or Buddhism would have attracted you the most, and why?
modelAnswer: Both religions rejected the caste system and the superiority of the Brahmins, so a person of a lower caste would be treated as equal and could even join the Buddhist Sangha. Their teachings were simple and were preached in Prakrit and Pali, the languages of the common people, rather than in Sanskrit. They did not require costly sacrifices or rituals performed by priests; salvation could be attained through one's own good conduct, such as following the Eightfold Path or the Triratnas.
keyPoints: Rejected caste distinctions; equality, open Sangha
Simple teachings in Pali/Prakrit, the people's languages
No costly rituals or sacrifices; no need for priests
Salvation through one's own good conduct

subject: History
text: In the absence of vast literary texts, inscriptions are crucial to understand the history of the Chola period. Justify the statement.
modelAnswer: Thousands of Chola inscriptions in Tamil and Sanskrit have been found on temple walls and copper plates. (1) The Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I describe in detail how village assemblies were elected and how they functioned, showing the system of local self-government. (2) Inscriptions on the Brihadeswara temple at Thanjavur and the meykirtis (eulogies) of kings record the conquests and achievements of rulers such as Rajaraja I and Rajendra I. (3) Copper plate grants, such as the Leyden and Tiruvalangadu plates, give the genealogy of the kings and details of land grants, taxes, temples, trade and social life.
keyPoints: Uttaramerur inscriptions: election and working of village assemblies
Temple inscriptions and meykirtis: conquests of Rajaraja I and Rajendra I
Copper plates (Leyden, Tiruvalangadu): genealogy, land grants, taxes
Throw light on temples, trade and social life

subject: History
text: Alauddin Khalji wanted to strengthen the state and maintain a large standing army. Propose any four revenue reforms he introduced to increase the resources of the royal treasury.
modelAnswer: (1) Land was measured and land revenue was fixed at half of the produce. (2) Land grants given as gifts, pensions and religious endowments (milk, inam and waqf) were taken back and brought under state control. (3) The privileges of the village headmen and revenue intermediaries (khuts, muqaddams and chaudhris) were abolished, so they had to pay taxes like others. (4) New taxes such as a house tax and a grazing tax (charai) were imposed, and a separate department, the Diwan-i-Mustakhraj, was set up to recover arrears strictly.
keyPoints: Land measured; revenue fixed at half the produce
Revenue-free land grants (inam, waqf) confiscated
Privileges of khuts, muqaddams and chaudhris abolished
House tax and grazing tax; Diwan-i-Mustakhraj to collect arrears

subject: History
text: Explain the Mansabdari System introduced by Akbar.
modelAnswer: Under the Mansabdari System, every official in the civil and military service was given a rank called a mansab, ranging from 10 to 10,000. Each mansab had two parts: zat, the personal rank and salary, and sawar, the number of horsemen the mansabdar had to maintain. Mansabdars were appointed, promoted and dismissed by the emperor himself, and the post was not hereditary. They were paid in cash or through the revenue of assigned lands (jagirs), and Akbar introduced the branding of horses (dagh) and a descriptive roll of soldiers (chehra) to prevent cheating.
keyPoints: Officials given ranks (mansabs) from 10 to 10,000
Zat = personal rank; sawar = number of horsemen to maintain
Appointed, promoted and dismissed by the emperor; not hereditary
Paid in cash or jagirs; dagh and chehra to prevent fraud

subject: History
text: Describe any three educational reforms introduced by Akbar.
modelAnswer: (1) Akbar set up many schools and colleges (maktabs and madrasas) where both Hindus and Muslims could study. (2) He changed the syllabus to include practical and secular subjects such as mathematics, agriculture, astronomy, medicine, history, logic and public administration, besides religious studies. (3) He set up a translation department (Maktab Khana) where Sanskrit works such as the Mahabharata (as Razmnama), the Ramayana and the Atharva Veda were translated into Persian. (4) He built a large imperial library and patronised scholars of all faiths.
keyPoints: Schools and madrasas for both Hindus and Muslims
New syllabus: mathematics, astronomy, agriculture, medicine, history, logic
Translation bureau: Sanskrit works (e.g. Mahabharata) into Persian
Imperial library and patronage of scholars

subject: History
text: The Great Bath highlights the Harappans' advanced understanding of water management. How did they make the tank waterproof and keep it clean?
modelAnswer: The Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro was a rectangular tank (about 12 m x 7 m and 2.4 m deep). It was made waterproof by using finely fitted burnt bricks laid in gypsum mortar, and by a layer of bitumen (natural tar) behind the walls and floor, which prevented leakage. It was kept clean because water was supplied from a well in an adjoining room, and an outlet drain in one corner allowed the dirty water to be emptied and the tank to be refilled with fresh water. Flights of steps at both ends led into the tank, and rooms around it were probably used for changing.
keyPoints: Burnt bricks laid in gypsum mortar
Layer of bitumen made it watertight
Water supplied from a nearby well
Outlet drain to empty dirty water and refill the tank

subject: History
text: Briefly discuss the three Rig Vedic assemblies that checked the powers of the king.
modelAnswer: (1) Sabha: a council of elders and important people of the tribe, which advised the king and also performed judicial functions. (2) Samiti: a general assembly of the people of the tribe, which discussed tribal affairs and could elect or even remove the king. (3) Vidatha: the oldest tribal assembly, in which both men and women took part, dealing with religious, social and military matters. Because the king had to consult these assemblies, his powers were not absolute.
keyPoints: Sabha: council of elders; advised the king, judicial work
Samiti: general assembly of the people; could elect/remove the king
Vidatha: oldest assembly; religious, social and military functions; women took part
Assemblies prevented the king from becoming absolute

subject: History
text: Discuss the Buddhist theory of Karma. How do Buddhism and Jainism differ in their understanding of Nirvana?
modelAnswer: Theory of Karma: Buddha taught that a person's present condition is the result of his own past actions (karma), and that his actions in this life determine his next birth; good deeds lead to a better birth and bad deeds to suffering. Desire keeps a person bound to the cycle of birth and death. Nirvana: In Buddhism, nirvana is the state of freedom from desire and suffering, ending the cycle of rebirth; it can be attained even in this life by following the Middle Path and the Eightfold Path. In Jainism, nirvana (moksha) is the liberation of the soul (jiva) from the bondage of karma, attained through the Triratnas and severe penance and self-mortification.
keyPoints: Karma: actions decide one's present and future births
Desire binds one to the cycle of birth and death
Buddhist nirvana: freedom from desire, via the Eightfold Path/Middle Path, possible in this life
Jain nirvana: freeing the soul from karma through Triratnas and severe asceticism

subject: History
text: Explain the literary importance of the Tirukkural as a source of the Sangam Age.
modelAnswer: The Tirukkural, written by Tiruvalluvar, is one of the most respected works of Tamil literature and is often called the "Tamil Veda". It has 1330 couplets in 133 chapters, divided into three sections: Aram (virtue), Porul (wealth and polity) and Inbam (love). It deals with ethics, politics, economics, duties of kings and ministers, and family life, and so throws light on the values and society of the time. Its teachings are universal and not tied to any one religion, and it has been translated into many languages.
keyPoints: Written by Tiruvalluvar; called the "Tamil Veda"
1330 couplets in 133 chapters
Three sections: Aram, Porul, Inbam
Universal ethical teachings; reflects society and polity of the time

subject: History
text: Briefly explain any two theories that explain the decline of the Harappan Civilisation.
modelAnswer: (1) Floods and change in the course of the Indus: repeated floods destroyed the cities, as layers of silt found at Mohenjo-daro show. (2) Climatic change and drying up of rivers: the climate became drier and rivers such as the Ghaggar-Hakra (Saraswati) dried up, leading to the decline of agriculture. (3) Aryan invasion: some historians believed that invading Aryans destroyed the cities, though this is now doubted. (4) Earthquakes and ecological imbalance due to deforestation may also have contributed.
keyPoints: Repeated floods / change in course of the Indus
Climate change and drying of rivers
Aryan invasion theory (now doubted)
Earthquakes and ecological damage

subject: History
text: Explain two measures adopted by Akbar to strengthen his alliance with the Rajputs.
modelAnswer: (1) Akbar entered into matrimonial alliances with Rajput ruling families; he himself married the princess of Amber (Jaipur). (2) He gave high ranks (mansabs) and important posts to Rajput chiefs such as Raja Man Singh and Raja Bhagwan Das, and allowed defeated Rajput rulers to keep their kingdoms. (3) He abolished the pilgrimage tax and the jizya, and allowed full religious freedom, which won the loyalty of the Rajputs.
keyPoints: Matrimonial alliances with Rajput royal families
High mansabs and posts to Rajputs (e.g. Raja Man Singh)
Defeated Rajputs allowed to keep their kingdoms
Abolished jizya and pilgrim tax; religious tolerance

subject: History
text: How does Fa-Hien's account help us understand the Gupta period?
modelAnswer: Fa-Hien, a Chinese Buddhist pilgrim, visited India during the reign of Chandragupta II and wrote the Fo-kwo-ki. He describes the administration as mild and efficient: taxes were light, there was no capital punishment and criminals were usually fined. He found the people prosperous, peaceful and happy, and noted charitable institutions such as free hospitals and rest houses, especially at Pataliputra. He also records that most people were vegetarian and did not drink wine, that there was religious tolerance, and that the Chandalas (untouchables) lived outside the towns.
keyPoints: Visited during Chandragupta II; wrote Fo-kwo-ki
Mild administration: light taxes, no capital punishment, fines
People prosperous; free hospitals and rest houses
Religious tolerance; vegetarianism; Chandalas lived outside towns

subject: History
text: Explain the electoral process (the Kudavolai system) used by the Cholas to elect members of the village assembly.
modelAnswer: According to the Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I, the village was divided into wards (about 30). Persons eligible to stand had to meet qualifications such as owning land and a house, being between 35 and 70 years of age, and having knowledge of the Vedas and good character; those who had served on a committee in the previous three years, had committed crimes or had not submitted accounts were disqualified. The names of eligible candidates of each ward were written on palm-leaf tickets and put in a pot (kudam). In a public meeting, a young boy drew one ticket for each ward, and that person was chosen. The members chosen formed committees (variyams) to manage village affairs.
keyPoints: Village divided into wards (about 30)
Qualifications: land and house ownership, age 35-70, learning and good character; disqualifications listed
Names on palm-leaf tickets put in a pot (kudam); a boy drew one per ward
Selected members formed committees (variyams)

subject: History
text: State any two architectural features of the Qutub Minar.
modelAnswer: The Qutub Minar in Delhi, begun by Qutub-ud-din Aibak and completed by Iltutmish, is about 72.5 metres high and has five storeys, each marked by a projecting balcony. It is built of red and buff sandstone (with marble in the upper storeys) and tapers from a wide base to a narrow top. Its walls have alternate angular and rounded flutings and are decorated with carved bands of Quranic verses in Arabic.
keyPoints: About 72.5 m high, five storeys with projecting balconies
Red and buff sandstone with some marble; tapers upward
Angular and rounded flutings
Carved bands of Quranic inscriptions

subject: History
text: Mention the teachings of Kabir as given in the Bijak.
modelAnswer: Kabir taught that God is one, whether called Rama or Rahim, and that devotion (bhakti) and love for God are the way to salvation. He opposed idol worship, pilgrimages, fasting and meaningless rituals of both Hindus and Muslims. He rejected the caste system and preached the equality of all human beings, stressed the importance of the guru, and worked for Hindu-Muslim unity. He also advocated a simple, honest life while remaining a householder.
keyPoints: God is one (Rama and Rahim are the same)
Opposed idol worship and empty rituals of both religions
Rejected caste; preached equality
Importance of the guru and Hindu-Muslim unity

subject: History
text: State the significance of Sufism on Indian society.
modelAnswer: (1) Sufi saints preached love, tolerance and equality of all, which brought Hindus and Muslims closer and promoted communal harmony. (2) They opposed the caste system and orthodoxy and served the poor, so their khanqahs and dargahs (such as that of Moinuddin Chishti at Ajmer) became centres visited by people of all faiths. (3) They enriched Indian culture: devotional music such as qawwali developed, and they wrote in local languages, helping the growth of Hindi and Urdu literature.
keyPoints: Promoted love, tolerance and Hindu-Muslim harmony
Opposed caste and orthodoxy; served the poor
Dargahs and khanqahs open to all faiths
Enriched music (qawwali) and regional/Urdu literature

subject: History
text: State any three occupations that existed during the Vedic Age.
modelAnswer: (1) Cattle rearing: cattle were the chief form of wealth, especially in the Early Vedic Age. (2) Agriculture: crops such as barley (yava), and later wheat and rice, were grown, and iron ploughshares were used in the Later Vedic Age. (3) Crafts: carpentry, metal work by smiths, weaving, leather work and pottery. (4) Trade: carried on mostly by barter, with cows and later nishka used as units of value.
keyPoints: Cattle rearing
Agriculture (barley, later wheat and rice)
Crafts: carpentry, metal work, weaving, pottery
Trade by barter

subject: History
text: State the contributions of Leonardo da Vinci in the field of art.
modelAnswer: Leonardo da Vinci (1452-1519), an Italian painter, was one of the greatest artists of the Renaissance. His paintings "The Last Supper" and the "Mona Lisa" are famous for their realism, use of perspective, and the play of light and shade. He studied human anatomy closely by dissecting bodies, which made his figures lifelike. He was also a sculptor, architect, engineer and scientist who made sketches of flying machines and other inventions, and is regarded as the ideal "Renaissance man".
keyPoints: Painted "The Last Supper" and the "Mona Lisa"
Realism, perspective, light and shade
Studied anatomy to draw lifelike figures
Also a scientist and inventor: a true "Renaissance man"

subject: History
text: State the contributions of William Shakespeare in the field of literature.
modelAnswer: William Shakespeare (1564-1616) was the greatest English poet and dramatist of the Renaissance. He wrote about 37 plays, including tragedies such as Hamlet, Macbeth, Othello and King Lear, comedies such as As You Like It and The Merchant of Venice, and historical plays such as Julius Caesar, as well as 154 sonnets. His works deal with human emotions and characters rather than religious themes, reflecting the humanist spirit of the Renaissance, and they greatly enriched the English language.
keyPoints: English poet and dramatist; about 37 plays and 154 sonnets
Tragedies: Hamlet, Macbeth, Othello, King Lear
Comedies and histories, e.g. As You Like It, Julius Caesar
Humanist themes; enriched the English language
